title: After the ten-thousand-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of migrant workers' daily life on camera
dek: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on photographing its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the ten-thousand-worker factory really did disappear, only a very few people had kept this archive.
why: This is not industry analysis; it is a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content people interested in the transformation of manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta's factory era disappeared.
skip: The show trailer and event notices at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value unimportant
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process to make manufacturing more stable and the people more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean — anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. There was no machine yet to replace them, but a person's value was already almost unimportant. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system that deliberately erases individual difference, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like climbing into a bandits' den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang starting station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed a window with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. More than thirty hours without being able to sit or drink water; after getting off, his belly was terribly swollen. At the Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold as a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan and said it was to Dongguan, then on the highway they demanded another ten for the expressway toll, and if you didn't pay, someone came up and slapped you, and in the end you were dumped in a wasteland with nothing around and made to change vehicles. He says he used the term for years and only understood what it meant last year.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 it was hard to find work; men had a far harder time than women, and factory recruitment notices stated outright that they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring notice by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people began dropping, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was left. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. Then he was told to spar with someone; the other man flashed a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, if you like it, then buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — in that era an enormous drain on him. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employees in tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a matter of technique, of getting a clear picture. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he found there was so much learning in photography and he had no standard by which to measure it, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: A model-contest photo passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete it
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding a model contest; the workers went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms they had made, and there was pole dancing too. In 2008 he changed position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience behind — and sent it to Tencent in time; it went up on the portal and drew tens of millions of clicks in a single morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss, a lover for the factory manager; the framing was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete it. Tencent said it could only be hidden, that other sites' viral reposting couldn't be stopped, and in the end served him a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had never planned to use it
points.body: On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he entered the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allows four minutes' rest after two hours; the place where they changed work clothes was hung all over with clean-room suits nobody was wearing, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow townsman heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the experience others had passed on to him when he was learning photography was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is never a good photo’, so he never used this one. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and it was unexpectedly made the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he admitted it had its own pull — different readers would have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his own photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people weren't wanted, Henan people weren't wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. Factories' information was separate then, with no networked computer systems, and social security didn't have to be paid, so this set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system wouldn't accept it — same ID number, same name, same registered household address, and the enterprise decided you were dishonest and zeroed out your years of service. He says this won't do: our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those many years of service are real. When even present-day life isn't secure, it's simply impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years off.

points.h: Density: he shot for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the density of migrant working life, which won an excellence award and the Alpa prize at the third Yingjishi Image Awards. Workers' assemblies shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung all over with clothes, from a distance airtight; and workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting with his phone every day, shooting security training, shooting any fellow worker he happened to see on the street, accumulating day by day, on and off for nearly 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he hadn't observed in that way; then one morning he found it so terrifying that even a switch looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as the warp, space as the weft: a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The complete thread he worked out was: time as the warp, space as the weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, and capital's impact on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a composite three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text and objects. Later he changed methods: starting from the keyword dagong (working for wages), he looked up ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, getting 322, and went into Baidu Images and began screenshotting all of them — this is the internet's understanding of dagong, to be presented together with his own understanding from actually shooting, in one huge exhibition space. He says this is us watching the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compares himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers get the credit, but it's the Sherpas who carry the loads — I'll just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets being transported; later it meant being cheated by middlemen and drivers who piled on charges along the way to work.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally known photography agency; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers one by one on its website.
A photography award organised by Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China; Zhan Youbing submitted work and had it shown as the lead image.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it wasn't about riding a train — you felt like you'd climbed into a bandits' den.
This is the era: we watch the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we arrive at certainly won't be poor; but if we can only see society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
